# THEORYs with `tags` `learning-and-conditioning`

*Topics — What a work is about. **Learning and conditioning** — how organisms learn from contingencies and consequences — Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning, reinforcement and reward learning in brains, habit and goal-directed control, behaviour analysis and relational responding. Not machine learning, which is learning-theory or the anthology (ADR-025).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) v2 | Expected tangible rewards for merely engaging in an interesting task lower later free-choice engagement with it | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). By their study-by-study account, Cameron and Pierce's rival analysis found the same for this contingency (performance-independent rewards, −0.29), while disputing nearly everything else. Their 2001 reply (LIT-562), read here, re-codes 145 studies and finds it again: rewards offered for doing an interesting task lowered free choice, −0.35 across 57 studies. Active: both sides of the dispute find this effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-049.md) v2 | Whether an external event lowers or raises intrinsic motivation depends on whether it is experienced as controlling or as information about competence | Cognitive evaluation theory, as tested by Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)) and summarized by Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)): rewards, feedback, deadlines and choice affect intrinsic motivation through their "functional significance". Controlling events shift the perceived locus of causality outward and undermine it; informational ones affirm competence and enhance it, but only with a sense of autonomy. The meta-analytic pattern fits, and controlling versus informational positive feedback differ by d = −0.78 in four studies. Mediation by felt control is untested for rewards. Its rival, Cameron, Banko and Pierce's account (LIT-562), finds rewards tied to a score or to beating others do not undermine. Neither side has tested mediation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-050.md) | Psychological inflexibility, in which verbal relations give private events aversive functions and make experiential avoidance a general strategy, is a transdiagnostic process in psychopathology | Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) model psychopathology as inflexibility: cognitive fusion supports experiential avoidance, which narrows behaviour. Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) give the mechanism: once a word stands in derived relation to an event it can carry that event's aversive functions, so private events become worth avoiding. Kashdan and Rottenberg ([LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md)) find inflexibility across depression and anxiety in cognitive, behavioural and physiological systems, and say its causal role is unknown. The evidence is correlational, small, mostly self-report and mostly from the model's authors, and the meta-analysis that would test it ([LIT-543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-543.md)) is unread, so Proposed. It is compatible with the loop account of disorder, not a rival to it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-062](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-062.md) | Model-based and model-free predictions both operate in instrumental and in Pavlovian learning, and which one controls behaviour follows their relative reliability, not the preference of a supervising system | Daw, Niv & Dayan ([LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md)) cast habitual and goal-directed instrumental control as model-free caching and model-based search, and let behaviour follow whichever estimate is less uncertain; simulations reproduce the effects of over-training, task complexity and reward proximity on devaluation. Dayan & Berridge ([LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md)) show from instant revaluation of a salt cue that Pavlovian prediction also has a model-based form, and suggest the same reliability arbitration there. Both controllers pursue the same ends; neither is the irrational one. The instrumental half is qualitative simulation; the Pavlovian half of the arbitration is a suggestion. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-154](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-154.md) | Whether an expected tangible reward lowers or raises later intrinsic motivation depends on how tightly its stated contingency ties it to performance and success | Cameron, Banko and Pierce (2001, [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md)), re-analysing 145 studies with contingencies coded by procedure. On interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermine later free choice when loosely tied to performance (for doing the task, for "doing well") or earned at less than the maximum; they do not when given for surpassing a score, and they enhance it when given for exceeding others. Read through social cognitive and behavioural theory: rewards tied to success carry competence. Proposed: the paper measures no mediator and pools control groups that differ in feedback. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md) | Adaptation by trial and error in a large system finishes in a practicable time only if partial adaptations are retained, and retention requires that the system not be fully joined: parts must be separated, at least temporarily, by constancies, and where later learning shares parts with earlier learning it destroys it | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md), Chs. 10–16. If all successes must occur at once, trials grow as (1/p)ᴺ; if each is kept once found, roughly as N/p. Keeping one needs no channel from what is still changing to what is already right, so a fully joined system, the Homeostat included, cannot accumulate; constancies cut a system into independent parts. Exact for the type-cases; the fit to brains is qualitative. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-324](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-324.md) v2 | A system adapts by trial and error to an environment whose effect on its essential variables it does not know only if a second feedback, through those variables, changes the parameters of its primary feedback; and if that feedback changes them whenever, and for as long as, an essential variable is outside its limits, every equilibrium the whole can reach is an adapted one | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md). Necessity is deduced from the trial-and-error rule against a Black Box environment; sufficiency from the theorem that a whole is at equilibrium only where every part is. The Homeostat shows it in a four-unit linear machine. The parameter changes are blind, and the account says nothing about how long the search takes, which is the subject of [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-484](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-484.md) | The brain implements hierarchical reinforcement learning with options: dorsolateral prefrontal cortex represents which option is active, dorsolateral striatum holds option-specific policies, orbitofrontal cortex holds option-specific values, and dopamine carries option-level prediction errors at subtask boundaries | Botvinick, Niv and Barto (2009), [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md), read in [NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md). Four proposed extensions of the actor-critic mapping, each matched to existing correlational findings, and predictions the authors say "call for further experimental scrutiny". The evidence for prefrontal coding of subtask segments is "only indirect". The mapping assumes pseudo-reward; other frameworks (HAM, MAXQ) would predict differently. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Chains of human function learners, each trained on the previous learner's responses, forget their starting function and in 28 of 32 families converge within a few generations to a positive linear function, the bias earlier studies report, whatever function trained the first learner; this is convergence to the learners' favoured function, not shown to be convergence to their prior | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. The bias was taken from earlier studies, not measured on these learners, and stationarity was not established. It supports the claim that human transmission chains settle on what learners favour in this task, not that they reach the Bayesian prior, and it cannot tell sampling learners from MAP learners. | Active |
| [THEORY-688](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-688.md) | In an actor-critic learner that can choose temporally extended options as well as primitive actions, options that fit the task speed learning, while options with ill-placed subgoals slow it, and options that fit an earlier layout keep the agent from finding a newly opened shortcut, so hierarchy helps only with the right subroutines | Botvinick, Niv and Barto (2009), [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md), read in [NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md). Toy simulations in a rooms domain with pre-trained options. Doorway options sped learning; window options slowed it; with a shortcut opened, primitive-only agents found the shortest path on 75% of runs while doorway-option agents never used it (mean 11.79 against 9.73 steps). It is a result about the model. That people or brains work this way is the separate, proposed account [THEORY-484](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-484.md). | Active |
| [THEORY-895](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-895.md) v2 | Incentive sensitization: repeated drug exposure can make the mesolimbic 'wanting' system lastingly hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, so that cue-triggered incentive salience grows, persists for years and even increases during abstinence, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall; sensitized 'wanting' can oppose the person's cognitive desire, and incentive salience can run without any reportable change in feeling | Berridge and Robinson (2016), [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md), read in [NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md) from the PMC author manuscript. Filed separately from [THEORY-893](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-893.md), which holds the liking–wanting dissociation, because what [QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md) and [CLAIM-433](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-433.md) need is the sensitization result: a ranking whose strength is re-keyed to cues, cut loose from both pleasure and the person's goals, and lasting. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-897](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-897.md) | Across seven computational learning studies selected without a systematic search, anxiety goes with altered adjustment of learning rate to uncertainty, mostly for aversive outcomes, while overall learning rate, choice consistency and outcome valuation show little relation to it | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022), [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md), read in full from the NIH author manuscript in [NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md). | [THEORY-900](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-900.md) | A systematic review of 116 studies of avoidance learning in healthy humans finds the evidence contradicting two-factor and other associative theories and favouring expectancy and inference-based accounts, but also finding residual avoidance after the outcome is visibly removed, which a purely inferential account does not predict | Mancinelli & Bach (preprint 2025; NBR 2026), [LIT-1477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1477.md), read in full in [NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md). The verdict is the authors' scoring of five theories against phenomena they rate for robustness; no model was fitted. They argue current paradigms are too simple to expose where inference gives way to Pavlovian control. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-901](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-901.md) | In laboratory avoidance learning in healthy humans, an avoidance response that remains available during extinction persists, in some participants for hundreds of unpunished trials, and keeps expectancy of the aversive outcome higher than in people denied it; the more effective and the cheaper the response, the slower it extinguishes | Mancinelli & Bach (preprint 2025; NBR 2026), [LIT-1477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1477.md), read in full from the PsyArXiv preprint in [NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md). | [THEORY-907](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-907.md) | In foraging tasks, higher stress or anxiety goes consistently with less exploration, and in one task with a predator to check for, people higher in somatic anxiety checked less and did worse, a reduction associated with greater aversion to detecting the predator | Chou, Wilson & Smith (preprint June 2024; NBR 2024), [LIT-1483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1483.md), read in full in [NOTE-1127](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1127.md). | [THEORY-910](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-910.md) | Brown, Price and Dombrovski propose, without a model run or data, that in aversive environments avoiding uncertain states keeps their uncertainty high and so perpetuates avoidance, that anxiety strengthens this loop by misreading noise as change, and that exposure works by reducing the uncertainty rather than an excess of learned threat | Brown, Price & Dombrovski (2023; preprint 2022), [LIT-1479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1479.md), read in full in [NOTE-1120](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1120.md). | [THEORY-912](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-912.md) | In a picture-based avoidance task, treatment-seeking patients with OCD or PTSD avoided a safety cue more than healthy controls and, after effective avoidance, still expected the aversive picture more; patients with panic disorder with agoraphobia or PTSD reported more relief when it was omitted; the groups did not differ in avoiding the danger cues | De Kleine et al. | [THEORY-914](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-914.md) | In fear conditioning, extinction does not erase the original threat association but adds a competing inhibitory one, which is why extinguished fear can return with time, a change of context, an unsignalled aversive event or renewed pairing | Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014), [LIT-1500](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1500.md), read in full from the PMC author manuscript in [NOTE-1137](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1137.md). The evidence is cited, not reported: the source is a clinical translation, and a promotion needs the primary literature. It does not show that exposure therapy in patients works by inhibitory learning alone. The authors allow that habituation also plays a part. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-915](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-915.md) | In a Markov decision process, an agent that evaluates actions as if it will fail to avoid danger at later steps, while in fact choosing optimally at each step, spreads threat value to states far from the danger and avoids early and widely, which reproduces qualitatively exaggerated threat appraisal, fear generalization and several laboratory findings associated with anxiety | Zorowitz, Momennejad & Daw (2020; preprint 2019), [LIT-1496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1496.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record in [NOTE-1136](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1136.md). A decision-theoretic argument and value-iteration simulations with a β-pessimistic Bellman equation. The misbelief is about the agent's own future control; the danger is represented correctly. No data are fitted. That learned values outlast correction of the misbelief is argued in the paper, not simulated, and is not part of this title. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-917](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-917.md) | Across computational studies of exploration in reward-based bandit tasks, mostly in sub-clinical samples and not yet replicated, directed exploration tends to rise with trait or cognitive anxiety and to fall with state or somatic anxiety, and random exploration shows no relation to anxiety | Chou, Wilson & Smith (preprint June 2024; NBR 2024), [LIT-1483](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1483.md), read in full from the PsyArXiv preprint in [NOTE-1127](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1127.md). A narrative review; the pattern is the authors' reading of about eight studies with different tasks, models and anxiety measures, with one failed replication and one null. The authors hedge it with "may" and "many results could be seen to suggest". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-920](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-920.md) | In three laboratory studies of healthy humans, offering a costless avoidance response for a stimulus never paired with the aversive outcome led people to use it, and withdrawing the response then raised their expectancy of the outcome for that stimulus, though not their skin conductance or startle in the one study that measured them; signalling of the response is a confound | Mancinelli & Bach (preprint 2025; NBR 2026), [LIT-1477](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1477.md), read in full in [NOTE-1134](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1134.md). | [THEORY-921](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-921.md) | How far fear falls during an extinction or exposure session, or across sessions, does not predict how much fear is expressed at follow-up, in animals, human laboratory samples and fearful human samples | Craske et al. The authors read it as "divergence in response systems": fear expressed during exposure and the learning that exposure produces need not change together. | [THEORY-922](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-922.md) v2 | Among 56 of 88 patients in one DBT intensive outpatient programme, kept because they finished a four-month cycle and gave enough diary data, skills-homework completion in months 1–3 correlated with larger falls in suicide and substance-use urges (r ≈ .35) and phone-coaching frequency with a larger fall in self-harm urges (r = .31); neither correlated with change in how often the behaviours occurred, and only homework separated patients with and without a target behaviour in month 4 | Edwards, Kober, Rinne, Griffin, Axelrod & Cooney (2021), [LIT-1480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1480.md), read in full in [NOTE-1121](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1121.md). | [THEORY-923](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-923.md) v2 | In one simulated T-maze task with hand-set parameters, run once per condition, an active inference agent's habit, learned by counting its own state transitions and policy choices, emerged from goal-directed behaviour, and once acquired it persisted, and reinforced itself, after the reward was devalued, while an agent devalued before acquisition switched at once | Friston, FitzGerald, Rigoli, Schwartenbeck, O'Doherty & Pezzulo (2016), [LIT-1476](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1476.md), read in full from the CC BY version of record in [NOTE-1138](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1138.md). | [THEORY-934](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-934.md) | Under Bush–Mosteller learning with negative payoffs, the continuous-time limit is a replicator term in benefits plus a probability-matching term, which alone drives choice probabilities to success probabilities | Börgers & Sarin (JET 1997; working paper 1993), [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md), read in full in [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md). When reinforcements may be negative, probability removed from a punished strategy is redistributed, and the limit is dp_j/dt = p_j(Ū_j* − p\|Ũ\|q) + Ū_j*(σ_j* − p_j). With payoffs of equal absolute size only the matching term remains. The limit is stated with its proof omitted. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-938](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-938.md) | Cross learning has the expected motion of the replicator dynamic and follows it on any finite horizon in the continuous-time limit, but for every learning speed the discrete process converges with probability one to a pure strategy profile, even in games where the replicator dynamic cycles | Börgers & Sarin (JET 1997; working paper 1993), [LIT-1505](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1505.md), read in full from the 1995 working paper in [NOTE-1149](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1149.md). Two players running Cross's rule with payoffs in (0, 1): expected change equals the discrete replicator step (Proposition 3); the slow-learning limit is the Taylor replicator dynamic at each finite time (Proposition 4); for every step size the process is absorbed in a pure profile with probability one (Proposition 5). The equivalence is pointwise in time, not uniform. | Proposed |
